title: System catalogs, extensibility, memory contexts and errors
one_liner: Postgres stores its own metadata in tables, caches it, calls functions through Datums, lets extensions hook in, and cleans memory and errors with contexts and longjmp.
analogy: A library keeps its own card catalog as books too. Memory contexts are labeled trash bins, each emptied in one go.
big_picture: System catalogs (pg_class, pg_proc, pg_type) are normal tables describing every table, function and type.
Reading catalogs on every query is slow, so catcache/syscache and relcache keep hot rows in memory.
Every SQL-callable C function takes PG_FUNCTION_ARGS and returns a Datum, a generic one-word value.
Extensions are shared libraries. They announce themselves with PG_MODULE_MAGIC and plug in via _PG_init and hooks.
palloc allocates inside a MemoryContext. Resetting or deleting a context frees everything in it at once.
ereport(ERROR) jumps back to a handler with longjmp. PG_TRY lets C code catch it.

flow.detail: Built-in catalog rows live in .dat files. genbki.pl turns them into bootstrap data at build time.
At backend start, the catalog cache and relation cache are initialised in phases.

flow.step: Code looks up a catalog row
flow.detail: Callers use SearchSysCache1, read columns with SysCacheGetAttr, then must ReleaseSysCache.
fmgr_info finds the C function pointer, built-in or from a shared library, and fills FmgrInfo.
Args travel in FunctionCallInfo. FunctionCall1Coll and friends wrap the call and return a Datum.
Library is loaded, _PG_init saves the old hook pointer and installs its own, e.g. ExecutorStart_hook.
palloc uses CurrentMemoryContext. MemoryContextReset or Delete frees the whole group.
ereport calls errstart and errfinish. ERROR does a longjmp to the PG_TRY or top-level handler.
Changes queue invalidation messages. Other backends run AcceptInvalidationMessages and drop stale entries.

diagram.claim: A catalog lookup flows through caches, then function calls reach built-in or extension code, with memory and errors managed on the side.

answer: Ordinary tables in the pg_catalog schema.
They store metadata: tables (pg_class), columns, types (pg_type), functions (pg_proc).
Postgres uses its own tables to describe itself.
interview.trap: Catalogs are not hidden C structs. They are real tables you can SELECT from.

interview.q: Why do we have syscache and relcache?
answer: Catalog lookups happen constantly. Going to disk or scanning each time is slow.
syscache caches single catalog rows by key.
relcache caches whole Relation descriptors with columns, indexes and more.

interview.q: What do you do after SearchSysCache?
answer: Read fields, using SysCacheGetAttr for variable columns.
Call ReleaseSysCache when finished.
The tuple is pinned in the cache and must not be modified.
interview.trap: Do not pfree the tuple or modify it in place. It belongs to the cache.

interview.q: What is a Datum and what does PG_FUNCTION_ARGS mean?
answer: Datum is a generic value, either the value itself or a pointer.
PG_FUNCTION_ARGS expands to FunctionCallInfo fcinfo.
Use PG_GETARG_INT32(n) to read args and PG_RETURN_INT32(x) to return.

interview.q: How does a SQL call reach C code?
answer: fmgr_info looks up the function in pg_proc and fills FmgrInfo.
Built-ins are found through fmgr_isbuiltin.
Others go through load_external_function in dfmgr.c.
The call itself passes a FunctionCallInfo.

interview.q: What do PG_MODULE_MAGIC and PG_FUNCTION_INFO_V1 do?
answer: PG_MODULE_MAGIC marks a library as built for this server version.
The loader checks it, and refuses mismatched libraries.
PG_FUNCTION_INFO_V1 declares a function with the version 1 calling convention.

interview.q: How does an extension change server behavior?
answer: _PG_init runs when the library loads.
It stores the previous hook, like prev_ExecutorStart, then sets its own.
Its hook calls the previous one, or the standard function if none.
CREATE EXTENSION runs scripts via CreateExtension in extension.c.
interview.trap: Forgetting to chain to the previous hook breaks other extensions.

interview.q: How does memory management work in Postgres?
answer: palloc allocates in CurrentMemoryContext.
pfree works on any chunk because the chunk knows its context.
Contexts form a tree under TopMemoryContext.
Resetting a context frees all its children and chunks.
interview.trap: Do not assume you must pfree everything. Contexts usually clean up for you.

interview.q: What happens on ereport(ERROR), and when do you use PG_TRY?
answer: errstart and errfinish build the error, then it longjmps out.
Normal code does not return from an ERROR.
PG_TRY catches it in C. Do cleanup in PG_CATCH or PG_FINALLY, then PG_RE_THROW.
Variables changed inside PG_TRY and used after should be volatile.
interview.trap: Swallowing an error without cleaning up leaves a broken transaction state.

contributor_tips: Read src/backend/utils/mmgr/README and src/backend/utils/fmgr/README first. They are short and explain the design.
Start by reading contrib/pg_stat_statements/pg_stat_statements.c to see hooks and _PG_init in a real module.
Always pair SearchSysCache with ReleaseSysCache and check for invalid tuples.
Be careful which memory context you allocate in. Wrong context causes leaks or dangling pointers.

glossary.meaning: Generic one-word value passed to and from functions.
A group of allocations that is freed together.
In-memory cache of catalog rows, looked up by key.
Cache of table and index descriptors.
A function pointer that extensions can override.
Macro block that catches ERROR in C code.
